extracted.intended_audience: newspaper readers, Congressional staff and policymakers following post‑war economic/foreign aid policy
extracted.subtask_short: reporting on US postwar economic policy
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting summarizing Congressional debate and executive proposals on post‑war price controls, allocation/priority powers, foreign relief buying, and disposition of surplus war machinery. Focus is on legislative amendments, administrative authorities requested, and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration anti‑inflation powers requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration’s anti‑inflation blueprint specifically requesting power to ration meat, gasoline and commodities as needed, as well as authority to buy up the entire wheat crop and to allocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a 10‑point program to Congress; requested 'standby authority' to be used only in acute circumstances. Framed as emergency powers to be invoked to curb the price spiral and protect industrial production and cost of living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed Allocation Program — covered items
rubrics_metrics.description: Harriman outlined items to be included in the allocation program: 1. Iron and steel, including rolled, forged, cast and drawn products; 2. Grain and grain products: rice, rice products, dried beans and peas, fats and oils of vegetable, animal or marine origin, livestock and poultry and their products, and milk and its products; 3. Freight cars and other railroad facilities and equipment regardless of ownership; 4. Tin and tin products; cinchona bark (quinine) held by any government agency; and nitrogenous fertilizer materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The measure would also give the president authority to allocate other materials if, after public hearings, he found that a shortage existed. The allocation program as described is presented as immediate priorities for governmental allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration extension for export controls and allocation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure would extend export controls, allocation and priority powers through March 31, 1950.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit temporal limit for the statutory authorities being requested; used to define the window in which allocation/priority powers would be in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to buy entire wheat crop
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration requested authority to buy up the entire wheat crop if it should be deemed advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such authority would enable government intervention in commodity markets to stabilize supplies/prices; under existing law the government must confer with industry and labor before exercising certain purchase powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodity Credit Corporation pooling / antitrust exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal would permit pooling of stocks and facilities and other joint operations without danger of anti‑trust laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to allow cooperative industry arrangements (pooling, joint operations) to manage shortages and distribution without triggering antitrust liability; presented as an instrumentality of an allocation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public‑hearing prerequisite for allocating additional materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The president would have authority to allocate other materials 'if, after public hearings, he found that a shortage' existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a procedural safeguard (public hearings) before expanding allocation powers beyond the specifically enumerated items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules/criteria for purchasing relief goods abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment: 'Any relief goods may be purchased abroad if their cost, upon delivery, is less than the cost of the goods delivered from the U.S.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion to minimize domestic price and supply impacts by buying relief goods where, delivered, they are cheaper than domestic purchase; ties relief procurement to comparative delivered cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25% cap for buying relief goods abroad when scarce at home
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment: 'Up to 25 per cent of the relief funds may be spent to buy ... goods abroad those goods are scarce in the U. S. and if their [delivered] cost [is] higher than the U.S. price.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits limited use of foreign procurement even for goods scarce at home, subject to a 25% ceiling on relief funds and a cost‑comparison condition; intended to balance foreign relief needs with domestic scarcity protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on relief buying in American markets (amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: House amendment (approved by voice vote) forbids relief buying in American markets at [text truncated in source].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects legislative intent to prevent relief procurement from worsening domestic shortages/prices by buying in U.S. markets; exact phrasing in the source is incomplete but the policy is a prohibition on domestic market purchases for relief under certain conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: President as 'watchman' over foreign aid's effect on the U.S. economy
rubrics_metrics.description: House added an amendment directing the President to make the regulations governing foreign relief buying so as to: (1) reduce the drain on commodities scarce in this country; and (2) cushion the effect of foreign purchases to prevent U.S. price rises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places an explicit executive responsibility to shape foreign aid procurement to minimize domestic economic harm; a statutory direction to balance aid objectives with domestic economic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation requirement with industry and labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Under existing legislation, the government must confer with industry and labor before [making purchases such as buying wheat].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement intended to consider domestic production/contractual obligations and to reduce unintended harms to industry and labor when exercising broad procurement powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold/conditions for invoking rationing or pricing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration/Interior officials: rationing or pricing authority would be used 'only in an acute situation' and 'full rationing is needed to meet the possibility of an emergency,' but 'there is no intention... to use [it] unless we really have to.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a high‑threshold/emergency standard for use of draconian powers (rationing/pricing), emphasizing avoidance unless necessary; also notes regional handling where shortages develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition view — restoration of controls risks black markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Meat Institute warned: 'The experience of the past ... rationing and price controls should amply demonstrate that restoration of controls simply would result [in] development of black markets, this time even super‑black markets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument to evaluate proposed control measures by their risk of creating underground markets and enforcement difficulties; used as a caution against reintroducing rigid controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: GOP alternative: voluntary industry agreements + export controls
rubrics_metrics.description: G.O.P. program (as tentatively outlined) would seek to halt the price spiral through other voluntary measures rather than through the 'standby authority' requested by the President; extend export controls as its only compulsory feature and provide funds for a voluntary program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames an evaluative contrast: prefer voluntary, industry‑wide agreements backed by export controls and financial incentives rather than compulsory rationing/allocation authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls on disposition of surplus war machinery — central sale office and precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: War Assets Administration machinery 'is being or has been declared surplus' and an investigator reported instructions that such machinery 'will be sold only through the Washington office.' Committee members demanded precautions so 'they will not be resold to the Soviet Government or its agents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural standard for surplus disposal: centralized sales channel (Washington office) and safeguards to prevent export/resale to adversaries; inspection and investigation by congressional committees emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy stance: block exports to Soviet Union and ensure safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative Rizley said he favored 'blocking all exports' to Russia and insisted War Assets Administration 'take proper precautions' so none of the surplus machinery would be resold to the Soviet Government or its agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hardline export‑control standard: legislative/administrative posture to prevent strategic items from reaching geopolitical adversaries; implies strict vetting of buyers and sale channels.
